newsitem.title: MEXICO: American Halloween strangles Mexico's Day of Dead.
newsitem.headline: American Halloween strangles Mexico's Day of Dead.

text.p: Mexican writers and intellectuals campaigned on Friday against Halloween, saying the imported American festivity is killing off one of their most sacred and ancient festivals, the Day of the Dead.
The Day of the Dead celebrations, which in many Mexican towns last from Oct. 31 to Nov. 2, are a powerful blend of European Catholic tradition and Mexican Aztec custom.
Following key dates in both cultures, November 1 is celebrated as the "Day of the Little Angels" in honour of dead children, and the next day departed adults are remembered.

Families decorate houses with the intensely bright orange cempasuchil flower used by the Aztecs to mourn the dead, children make shrines in homes to the departed, bakeries produce "Dead Man's Bread" and shops sell little candy skulls.
Above all, Mexican families journey to cemeteries to offer food, drink, cempasuchil flowers and conversation to their dead loved ones at their graves between November 1 and 2.
But, academics and writers said on Friday that Mexico's ancient Day of the Dead celebrations were under threat as never before from imported American Halloween festivities.

Streets in Mexico City, Monterrey and other large Mexican cities were full of children on the night of October 31 trick- or-treating in witches' disguise and shops were stuffed full of imported American disguises and other Halloween gear.
Middle-class kids went to Halloween parties at their friends' houses, scared each other with American-style costumes and collected imported candies rather than cempasuchil.

"The Day of the Dead is threatened," writer and social columnist Guadalupe Loaeza told Reuters. "Halloween is gaining ground. Ten or fifteen years ago you would never have seen any Halloween celebration at all. Now shops are full of it."

Mexico's official news agency Notimex agreed. "An unquestionable fact: the Anglo-Saxon custom of Halloween has displaced the Day of the Dead in urban centres of the country -- where two-thirds of our population live," it mourned in a dispatch on Friday.
Some Mexicans want to stage a counter-attack before the Day of the Dead is reduced to a tourist stunt in a few isolated rural towns.

Writer and ecologist Homero Aridjis issued an anti- Halloween manifesto, the Catholic Church in the northern border state of Chihuahua has been handing out leaflets with the slogan "Say No to Halloween" and the Education Ministry has advised teachers to stick to Day of the Dead topics in the classroom.

"Halloween has as its background a materialist society like that of the United States which makes any event the object of marketing," the Church in the Chihuahua city of Ciudad Juarez said in its leaflet, distributed to 50,000 homes. "It is a vulgar and absurd copy of the Christian tradition of venerating the dead".
Recalling Halloween's pagan origins in Celtic Britain, the leaflet told parents: "Let's not allow our children to get involved in non-Christian practices".

Aridjis's manifesto, denouncing Halloween as "cultural contamination", said the invasion of the pagan American celebration was yet another reflection of ever-greater Mexican dependence on the United States.

As Mexico's economy has opened up to foreign investment over the past 10 years, McDonalds burger restaurants, Wal-Mart hypermarkets, U.S.-style shopping malls and other Americana have been steadily advancing across the country, flattening Mexican tradition and culture in their wake.
